cur:manuscripts-girona-beatus-lamb-four-.summary: In a medallion at the top, labelled 'Agnus', the Lamb with a cross-nimbus stands holding a cross-staff, while the four living creatures summon in turn the four horsemen, who ride across the coloured bands of the page below: the archer on a white horse, the rider with a sword, the rider with scales, and Death. The Lamb is shown as the one who opens the seals.
facts: With 184 surviving miniatures on 284 leaves, it is described as one of the most richly decorated and best documented of the Beatus commentaries.

The Girona Beatus was completed on 6 July 975 for an abbot Dominicus, probably at the monastery of Tábara; unusually, its painters are named: 'Ende, woman painter and servant of God', and the monk-priest Emeterius.
cur:manuscripts-girona-beatus-lamb-four-.notes: The Commons title ('Jesus and the Apostles looking down on the Earth') does not describe the image; the subject is the opening of the first four seals. Christ appears as the Lamb. Folio not given.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Within a purple medallion, the haloed Christ stands holding a cross-staff, while a dark demon with a spear lurks outside at the left and arrows fly through the air at the right. The verses below speak of 'the arrow that flieth by day … the destruction that wasteth at noonday'.
facts: Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-36-christ.summary: The nimbed Christ-Logos with six angels appears in the heavens above the bearded psalmist, enthroned before a lectern with a book and scales beneath a personified sun: 'he shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light'. Around them the drawing illustrates the psalm's sayings — the righteous fed in the days of famine, an angel upholding a man about to fall, and provisions shared out to the needy. It is a pictorial commentary on trust in the Lord.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-36-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-49-christ.summary: On a hill in the centre the nimbed Christ-Logos, blessing and holding a book, stands in a mandorla among angels while fire falls from heaven and burns on the hillsides: 'our God shall come ... a fire shall devour before him'. The psalmist and an angel gather the saints, and the rising and setting suns mark the ends of the earth. The scene has the character of a Last Judgement.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-106-chris.summary: A half-figure of the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos with three angels, sun and moon fills the centre of the heavens, and the bearded psalmist stands below with outspread hands between thrones and groups of elders, 'praise him in the assembly of the elders'. Walled 'cities for habitation' and ships on the sea surround the scene. The composition is a hymn to the Lord's deliverance of the wanderer and the seafarer.

vam:O14726.summary: The veiled Virgin sits at the centre of this bronze relief, gazing down at the dead body of her Son stretched across her knees; her right hand supports his shoulder and her left rests on his waist. Christ's head falls back, his long hair hanging loose, while two small winged angels stand on clouds at either side with their hands joined in prayer. The tender, sorrowful image once formed the door of a tabernacle, guarding the reserved Sacrament behind the figure of Christ's sacrificed body.
facts: The relief was formerly attributed to the Paduan sculptor Giovanni Minelli, but is now thought to have been made at Ferrara; its style and figure types relate closely to works in the circle of Niccolò Baroncelli (d. 1453).
It is cast in bronze in low relief, with traces of gilding, and measures about 56 by 49 cm (V&A).
vam:O14726.notes: Worklist year (850) was an error: this is a 15th-century Italian work (V&A: Ferrara, third quarter of the 15th century), so it moves out of the 1st–10th-century batch. Acquired in London (inv. 5469-1859).

feat:romanos-ivory.summary: Christ stands on a raised pedestal, taller than the human figures, and lays his hands on the heads of an emperor and empress, crowning them; inscriptions name them as Romanos and Eudokia. The image expresses the Byzantine conviction that earthly rulers receive their authority directly from Christ, the true King. Its elegant, elongated figures and refined drapery make it the namesake of an entire group of court ivories.
facts: Two Byzantine imperial couples bore these names, so scholars still debate whether it shows Romanos II and Bertha-Eudokia (945–949) or Romanos IV and Eudokia Makrembolitissa (1068–1071).
Bertha, the daughter of King Hugh of Italy, took the name Eudokia on her marriage to the young Romanos II.
The emperor is shown beardless, which many scholars take as support for identifying him with the young Romanos II, crowned as a boy in 945.
Its style defines the 'Romanos group' of ivories, to which the Harbaville Triptych also belongs.
